1 Mission, mandate and management
EEA′s mission statement
The EEA aims to support sustainable development and to help achieve significant
and measurable improvement in Europe′s environment through the provision of
timely, targeted, relevant and reliable information to policy-making agents and
the public.
EEA′s legal mandate
The EEA is a decentralised agency of the European Union. The EEA-Eionet
Regulation (1) established the EEA as an independent EU body with its own legal
personality and for an indefinite period. The Agency′s founding regulation also
established the European Environment Information and Observation Network
(Eionet); and includes the provision that the Agency is open to countries that are
not members of the EU. The EEA's overall mandate, established in the EEA-Eionet
Regulation is to help the European Community and the EEA member countries make
informed decisions about improving the environment, integrating environmental
considerations into economic policies and moving towards sustainability in
coordination with Eionet.
EEA′s objective
To achieve the aims of environmental protection and improvement laid down by
the Treaty and by successive Community action programmes on the environment,
as well as of sustainable development, the objective of the Agency and Eionet
shall be to provide the Community and the Member States with: ′objective, reliable
and comparable information at European level enabling them to take the requisite
measures to protect the environment, to assess the results of such measures and to
ensure that the public is properly informed about the state of the environment, and to
that end the necessary technical and scientific support.′

Environmental management
To minimise its environmental impacts and continually improve its performance,
the EEA has in place an environmental management system (EMS), as an
integral part of EEA management plan and is designed to make its environmental
responsibilities clear to employees. The EEA′s EMS is set up in accordance with the
requirements of the EU′s Eco-Management and Audit Scheme (EMAS) Regulation
and the EN ISO 14001:2015 standard. EEA is EMAS certified since 2005. Since
2020, the EEA environmental policy is to become a climate neutral and resource
efficient organisation.
In this context the EEA is committed to:
• continuously improving energy and material efficiency;
• maintaining staff awareness and understanding of work-related
environmental issues;
• encouraging sharing and implementation of ideas for environmental improvement;
• making use of the Agency′s own data, experience and accumulated knowledge in
managing environmental performance;

• influencing and inspiring other EU bodies and institutions in their
environmental endeavours;
• complying with all environmentally relevant legislation and regulations of our
host country.
The environment policy covers all Agency operations and staff — both at the EEA′s
premises and on missions. The policy also applies to all other persons working at the
Agency′s premises.
The Environmental management programme details for each significant
environmental aspect (e.g. electricity consumption, paper consumption,
greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, etc) the source of impact, an action plan and
annual targets, also referred to as performance indicators. The environmental
management programme is updated and approved in the first quarter of every year.
The environmental management programme is published as part of the annual
environmental statement report on the EEA website.
As part of the pathway to climate neutrality and resource efficiency by 2030, the EEA
will specify a percentage reduction of its greenhouse gas emissions to ensure its
climate neutrality goal is met by 2030.
EEA's environmental performance (of the previous year) is detailed in the annual
environmental statement, together with the updated target and action plan for the
present year. See Annex 6 for further details on EEA′s Environmental management.

2 General context
2.1 Policy developments
The year 2026 will be the second year of the new European Union (EU) policy
cycle. Priorities for this were defined in key policy documents published in the
course of 2024, including the Political Guidelines and the Mission Letters to the
Commissioners. These policy documents confirm the European Green Deal (EGD),
the priorities of the Eighth Environment Action Programme (8th EAP) and the delivery
of the objectives of the United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
as horizontal priorities for the European Commission (EC). However, given the shift in
the political landscape and geopolitical developments, more prominent issues have
now emerged for the EC: competitiveness alongside security and resilience. In this
context, simplifying and reducing administrative burdens for companies and Member
States are being highlighted as key objectives.
Furthermore, there is an emphasis on the importance of dialogue with citizens and
stakeholders; this includes consideration for how policies are implemented on the
ground. There is growing awareness that implementing the EGD agenda requires
significant public and private investment and effort, including from citizens, and that
it will be crucial to address the societal impacts of policies to ensure a fair transition.
Early in 2025, within the first 100 days of this governance period of the EC, these
priorities were translated and further refined into strategic documents, setting the
scene for what can be expected in the coming period and defining the broader policy
framework in which environment and climate policies are likely to be developed.
They include:
• the Competitiveness Compass, built around the three pillars of the Draghi report:
(1) closing the innovation gap with the US and China; (2) developing a joint plan for
decarbonisation and competitiveness — which was further detailed in the Clean
Industrial Deal; (3) increasing security and reducing dependencies;
• the EU Preparedness union strategy, as a follow-up to the Niinistö report, to
enhance Europe′s capability to prevent and respond to emerging threats, with a
clear recognition that climate and environment risks need to be part of the picture.
As a follow-up, the EC launched a first series of concrete policy initiatives in 2025.
These initiatives included, amongst other things:
• the water resilience strategy;
• a proposal relating to the 2040 climate target;
• a roadmap for nature credits;
• a bioeconomy strategy;
• an Economic Security package that includes the ResourceEU initiative, as a
follow-up to the Critical Raw Materials act;

• a simplification omnibus proposal specifically related to the environment;
• a European Grids package.
Other initiatives are still expected to be launched by the European Commission
in 2025:
• a Health package and a Clean Industrial Deal implementation package;
• an automotive package that includes a revision of the CO standards for cars and

vans, and a proposal on greening corporate fleets;
• a targeted revision of the Regulation on the Registration, Evaluation, Authorisation
and Restriction of Chemicals (possibly in 2026).
These initiatives will be further discussed with co-legislators and other stakeholders
throughout 2026 whilst preparations continue for the launch of new initiatives in
the coming year, as announced in the Commission work programme 2026. This
includes an enabling climate and energy framework to for the decade ahead to
support the implementation of the 2040 climate target and the objective to bring
down energy prices for households and companies, a Circular Economy Act to foster
demand and supply of circular products, all closely linked to the Clean Industrial
Deal, and a European integrated framework for climate resilience. Furthermore, a
Livestock strategy, a Vision 2040 for fisheries and aquaculture and the Ocean Act are
expected to be launched, whilst in the meantime the implementation of the Water
Resilience Strategy will continue, with a Digital Action Plan and a Water Resilience
Platform to mobilise all actors, drive water efficiency and strengthen the sector′s
competitiveness. The announced European strategy on sustainable tourism may also
be relevant in this regard. Directly or indirectly, EEA knowledge and support will be
extremely important for all of these initiatives.
Furthermore, on 16 July 2025, the EC presented its proposals for the next multiannual
financial framework (MFF) 2028-2034. The proposals transform the structure of the
budget quite fundamentally by merging and transferring several existing funds into
′national and regional partnerships′ and by creating a new ′competitiveness fund′.
The EEA would be funded under the competitiveness pillar of the next MFF. The EC
has set a 35% dedicated target for climate and environmental spending, roughly
EUR 700 billion. At the same time, it will also introduce an enhanced system to
monitor EU spending and results relating to green objectives. Negotiations will likely
accelerate throughout 2026, paving the way for a reorientation of EU resources to
deliver on the new policy priorities.
The acceleration of climate change, biodiversity loss and pollution and the
consequences for nature, food production, water security, energy security and
the economy require the EU to further reinforce its policies in the coming years in
response to the increasing climate and ecosystem impacts which are anticipated.
The EU will also have to reinforce its policies in the coming years in response
to expected worsening environment- and climate-related impacts on health.
This is happening in a challenging international environment, where geopolitical
considerations are growing in importance. In cooperation with Eionet, its country
network, the EEA will continue to play a significant role in providing information
about progress with the green transition and knowledge to inform solutions.

2.2 Development of new tasks
This section provides an overview of all the new tasks for the EEA in the current
MFF 2021-2027, which include a reinforcement of the EEA′s resources to deliver
them. The section comprises:
• new tasks already included in the EEA′s work programme and budget
(Section 2.2.1);
• potential new tasks currently under discussion to include in a legislative initiative
(Section 2.2.2);
• new tasks which have been contracted with the Commission via grant, contribution
and service-level agreements (Section 2.2.3).
Section 3.3, ′Human and financial resources outlook for the years 2026-2028′,
provides an overview of the EEA′s resources (staffing and budget) which are being
reinforced to deliver the new tasks. Annex 11 provides a list of the EEA′s grant,
contribution and service-level agreements.
2.2.1 Developments up to 2025
In the current MFF, the EC has specified a variety of new tasks for the EEA via
legislative acts, in particular to meet the ambitions of the EGD. These acts have
included legislative financial statements (finance fiches) specifying additional staff
and financial resources for the EEA to deliver on the new tasks. Where appropriate,
the acts have been bundled into packages, with the finance fiche for the entire
package attached to one of the legislative acts in the package.
Two legislative packages were adopted by the budgetary authorities during 2025:
The Soil Monitoring Directive in October and the One Substance One Assessment
in November.
An overview of the two packages is given below:
• The objectives of the Soil Monitoring Directive include putting in place a solid and
coherent soil monitoring framework for all soils across the EU and continuously
improving soil health in the EU with a view to achieving healthy soils by 2050 and
maintaining soils in healthy condition.
• The one substance, one assessment (OSOA) package specifies the development
of dataflows for collecting human biomonitoring and indoor air quality data,
supporting the development of the common data platform for chemicals and the
establishment of an early warning system for chemical substances. The package
specifies four TA and two CA posts, including one TA post for the Waste Framework
Directive (WFD).
Seven legislative packages specifying additional tasks and resources for the EEA
were adopted between 2021 and 2024. These packages are listed and described
briefly below:
• The EU Nature Restoration Regulation, formally adopted in June 2024, is part of a
plan for the restoration of nature in the EU. The plan will help improve the health of
existing and newly protected areas and restore the diversity and resilience of nature
in all landscapes and ecosystems. The EEA has key roles throughout the lifecycle
of the regulation; these range from designing reporting formats in the pre-reporting

phase to collecting data during the reporting phase and assessing the impacts of
the national restoration measures.
• A recast European Pollutant Release and Transfer (E-PRTR) Regulation, adopted
in April 2024, has resulted in a substantially improved reporting mechanism and
consolidation of a streamlining exercise, initiated in 2014, to feed into the European
Industrial Emissions Portal (IEP).
• The EU Carbon Removals and Carbon Farming (CRCF) Regulation (EU) 2024/3012
entered into force in December 2024. It aims to create an EU-wide voluntary
framework for carbon removal certification. The EEA′s tasks in this area include
supporting the EC in establishing and implementing certification methodologies,
quality criteria and monitoring, reporting and verification of carbon credits and
maintaining an overview of certification scheme methodologies. This initiative was
packaged with an initiative for expanded monitoring of emissions from heavy-duty
vehicles (HDVs). The EEA′s tasks in relation to HDVs include implementing the
reporting system, delivering quality control and assurance and providing a technical
helpdesk for reporters.
• The revised Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry (LULUCF) Regulation,
which sets out the EU target for net removals in the LULUCF sectors by 2030 as
well as binding national targets, requires substantial support from the EEA. The
EEA′s tasks in this area include reviews of Member States′ LULUCF GHG inventory
data, accounting and application of flexibility rules, verifying the Member States′
technical corrections for the Forest Reference Level, analysis of annual preliminary
progress towards targets, evaluation of correction actions proposed by Member
States and supporting Member States with identifying options to increase and
ensure long-term storage of carbon removals.
• The EEA is redeveloping and will maintain the two databases on Seveso
establishments and major industrial accidents (i.e. the online Seveso Plants
Information Retrieval System (eSPIRS) and the online Major Accident Reporting
System (eMARS)), as a result of an implementing act on the reporting requirements
relating to the Seveso III Directive. This work commenced in 2023, with operational
implementation planned from 2026 onwards.
• The EEA hosts the secretariat of the European Scientific Advisory Board on Climate
Change (ESABCC) and supports reporting on progress towards climate neutrality
and monitoring and evaluation of progress on adaptation. These tasks were
established under the European Climate Law (Regulation (EU) 2021/1119), which
came into force in 2022.
• The EEA has undertaken several new tasks as set out in 8th EAP legislation, which
came into force in 2021.
2.2.2 Foreseen new tasks in 2026 to 2028
Three further packages have been included in the EEA′s 2026 budget. However,
the EC holds these budgets and posts in reserve, only transferring them to the EEA
once the acts have been formally adopted. Adoption of the Zero Pollution Package
is anticipated in the first quarter, but progress on Green Claims remains uncertain.
The European Commission has recently announced the Forest Monitoring Law
proposal will be withdrawn and it appears with this status in the Commission′s 2026
work programme; this was too late to remove it from the 2026 budget, but it has been
removed from the budgets for 2027 and 2028.

An overview of the three packages is given below:
• The Zero Pollution Package includes three legislative proposals: a revision of
the list of groundwater and surface water pollutants, a proposal for a revision
of the Urban Waste Water Treatment Directive (UWWTD) (adopted) and a
proposal for a revision of air quality legislation (adopted). The new tasks include
developing a platform for integrated water management and reporting, support
for new monitoring activities for the revised UWWTD and new monitoring,
reporting, exchange of information and assessment and support activities for the
implementation of the revised Air Quality Directive. The package specifies a total
of five temporary agent (TA) posts and three contract agent (CA) posts. Three of
the TA posts will deliver the integrated water management reporting under the
Environmental Quality Standards Directive (EQSD), two TA posts will deliver air
quality objectives, one CA post will focus on urban wastewater treatment and two
CA posts on water reuse. The EEA will redeploy one TA post internally for the EQSD.
• The Green Claims Directive, on substantiation and communication of explicit
environmental claims, sets out monitoring requirements to provide an overview of
faulty environmental claims and labels. Member States will compile information on
these and report them to the EEA which, in turn, will publish a report assessing the
evolution of environmental claims in each Member State and the EU as a whole.
These reports will be released every second year. The finance fiche specifies one
TA and one CA post.
• The Forest Monitoring Law proposal aims to ensure coherent high-quality
monitoring of forests, making it possible to track progress towards achieving EU
policy objectives and targets that concern forests, including progress in relation
to biodiversity, climate and crisis response. The proposal aims to improve risk
assessment and preparedness, support evidence-based decision-making by land
managers and public authorities and promote research and innovation. The finance
fiche specifies one TA and two CA posts.
The EC is working on further legislative initiatives, which would specify additional
tasks for the EEA and additional resources to deliver them, though these resource
implications are not reflected in the draft 2026 budget. Information on these
initiatives is provided below.
The EEA has been discussing the feasibility and resource implications of establishing
a renewed environmental footprints database, linked to a range of legislation related
to product policy. Securing the necessary resources for this remains very uncertain at
this stage, with the Green Claims Directive mentioned above being a potential vehicle,
should it be adopted.
The EEA is in the discussion with the European Commission about financing the
future European climate risks assessment (EUCRA) to become a core task for the
EEA. The first and the second editions of EUCRA have been financed by the service
level agreements. The first edition was delivered in 2024, resourced by a service
level agreement with the EEA. The second edition of EUCRA will be delivered in
2028. The work on the European Climate Adaptation Platform (Climate-ADAPT) is
currently financed by the EEA with the support from DG CLIMA for the specific IT
developments. The current model requires upgrades in order support the preparation
and implementation of the European climate resilience legislation which is currently
under preparation.
The regular European climate risk assessments should become a core task for the
EEA, ongoing from the first risk assessment which the EEA delivered in 2024, resourced
by a service-level agreement (SLA) with the DG for Climate Action (DG CLIMA).

The financing of the Climate-ADAPT will need to be revised depending on the role of
the Climate-ADAPT in the future legislations.
With the expected revision of the Governance Regulation 2018/1999 by the end of
2026, there may be changes to the governance framework that would be relevant for
the work of the EEA.
Finally, the European Court of Auditors special report 18/2023 outlined the
outstanding issue of supporting Member States′ commitments to achieving 2030
targets. This particularly referred to the importance of consistent information on the
expected cost and effects of national policies to achieve climate targets. The EEA
has been working with Member States and member countries to strengthen their
reporting on national climate policies and measures. It will continue to do this.
2.2.3 Grant, contribution and service-level agreements
The EEA′s work includes engagements with Directorates-General (DGs) across
the EC that are financed through grant, contribution and service-level agreements
(the funding is referred to as externally assigned revenue). The EEA welcomes this
engagement on a broader range of activities which complement its core-funded
work programme.
The primary instrument used for these engagements is the SLA: the EEA currently
has agreements with seven separate DGs and is in negotiations for an eighth
to commence during 2025. The EEA recommends the use of SLAs over other
instruments, particularly for responding quickly to short-term needs: they are an EC
standard and lighter legal instrument that allow the parties to more quickly and easily
negotiate and commence. Furthermore, in contrast to other instruments, they provide
greater flexibility to allow the parties to respond quickly to evolving or changing
operational demands and ensure the EEA is able to fully recover its direct and indirect
costs in a manner that is transparent, simple and equitable for both parties.
The EEA is engaged with two DGs in long-term activities funded by contribution
agreements: with the DG for Neighbourhood and Enlargement Negotiations (DG NEAR)
for the EEA's engagement with the Western Balkans and Energy Community and with
the DG for Defence Industry and Space (DG DEFIS) for the civil Earth observation
component of the EU space programme (Copernicus); the initial agreement for the EC
to support Earth observation services was made in 2007.
Whilst the above instruments allow a broader engagement with the EC, there are
also disadvantages. The short-term nature of the agreements hinders knowledge
retention and use, disrupt continuity and frustrate the recruitment and retention of
qualified staff. Additional contracting, reporting, control and audit requirements also
place a heavy administrative reporting burden on core EEA resources, particularly
administrative, information technology (IT) and communication support functions.
The EEA has therefore proposed to the EC that the agreements funding ongoing
activities are replaced and included in the EEA's core work programme and
EU subvention.
The section below provides a list and brief description of the agreements that are
currently in force between the EEA and the EC. Additional information, including
resources and budgets, is provided in Annex 11, ′Plan for grant, contribution and
service-level agreements′.

Service-level agreements
• The work on the second edition of the European climate risk assessment (EUCRA2)
has been financed by the SLA with the DG for Climate Action (DG CLIMA). The
EUCRA2 will be published in Q3/2028 and will focus on assessing the climate risk
Europe is facing, address the risk ownership in detail and introduce the concept
of the resilience solutions spaces for policy making. The EUCRA2 builds on the
methodology of the first edition of EUCRA (EUCRA1).
• There is an ongoing six-year engagement with the DG for Research and Innovation
(DG RTD) for ′Mainstreaming GEOSS [the Global Earth Observation System
of Systems] data sharing and management principles in support of Europe′s
environment′ under the Horizon Europe programme. The engagement commenced
in December 2020 and the current agreement (EuroGEO 24) continues to
March 2027.
• There is a seven-year agreement (August 2021-December 2028) with the DG for
Health and Food Safety (DG SANTE) to support health content developments and
maintain the European climate and health observatory platform; this agreement
was amended in 2024 to include an additional task to support the monitoring of
serious cross-border threats to health.
• There is a three-year agreement with the DG for Regional and Urban Policy
(DG REGIO), which began in January 2022, to support the implementation of
regional and urban environmental indicators and analysis, addressing regional
and urban land use and various aspects of air pollution in Europe.
• There is a three-and-a-half-year agreement, which commenced in May 2022 with
DG CLIMA supporting the EU Mission on Adaptation to Climate Change (as part
of the EU Horizon Europe programme), by designing and implementing a support
system (in the form of a new set of features and tools included in Climate-ADAPT)
tailored to the specific needs of the mission and preparing mission web pages for
the associated mission implementation platform.
• There is a four-year agreement with Eurostat, which commenced in January 2023,
to cooperate on a variety of topics, including better use by the EEA of Eurostat data
and accounts and the creation of new geo-spatial data sets based on Copernicus
land monitoring service (CLMS) products in support of EU ecosystem accounting
and other Eurostat reporting obligations (e.g. on SDGs). To achieve these aims,
the whole CLMS portfolio will be analysed, with special emphasis on Corine
Land Cover and its successor, the Extended Corine Land Cover Programme and
high-resolution layers.
• There is a two-year agreement with the Joint Research Centre (JRC), which
commenced in December 2023, to deliver tasks supporting the Nitrates Directive.
The agreement will provide the required technical and scientific assistance to the
EC for the 2023-2025 reporting cycle with a view to a potential transfer of this
responsibility from the JRC to the EEA.
• There is a four-year agreement, which commenced in May 2024, with the DG for
Maritime Affairs and Fisheries (DG MARE) to support the monitoring of the EU
Mission: Restore our Oceans and Waters by 2030. The EEA is responsible for the
development of an indicator-based monitoring framework to track and assess
the impact of the EU Mission activities in achieving objectives and targets of
relevant EU policies. Monitoring assessment reports are published on an annual
basis through a dedicated science-policy interface on WISE Marine. The work is

conducted by the EEA in close collaboration with DG MARE and in consultation with

The EEA is currently negotiating two further SLAs:
Firstly, with the DG for Mobility and Transport (DG MOVE) to support CountEmissions
EU, which aims to create two consistent EU-wide databases and third-party

Secondly, Disaster Risk Reporting with European Civil Protection and Humanitarian

Contribution agreements
The Copernicus contribution agreement with DG DEFIS continues the EEA′s
development of the CLMS and the coordination of Copernicus′ access to in-situ
data. The EEA originally engaged in 2007 with the DG for Internal Market, Industry,
Entrepreneurship and SMEs (DG GROW) for the delivery of Corine Land Cover.
The current agreement (implementation period November 2021-December 2028 with
a budget of EUR 142.5 million) succeeds five previous agreements with DG GROW.
The main challenges for the current implementation phase include maintaining
continuity within the operational service while also ensuring a better response to
policy requirements, such as those addressed in the EGD, and wider uptake by the
broad community of users (e.g. authorities and scientific communities).
The EEA′s engagement with the Western Balkans commenced in 2002 via an
agreement with the DG for Enlargement. This engagement has continued through
12 agreements with DG Enlargement followed by DG NEAR. The EEA′s engagement
expanded significantly in 2023, in response to a request from the Energy Community
secretariat for the EEA to take on a role specified by an adaptation of the Regulation
on the Governance of the Energy Union and Climate Action in the Energy Community;
this role is to support reporting by the six Western Balkan countries, as well as
Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine. The EEA therefore entered into two contribution
agreements with DG NEAR to cover both the Energy Community tasks and the
continued cooperation with the Western Balkan countries on green agenda activities.
These agreements expire soon, and the EEA is close to concluding a further three-year
contribution agreement with DG ENEST to continue the Energy Community and
Western Balkan tasks, and engage in similar tasks with Moldova. The agreements
are funded under the Instrument for Pre-accession Assistance (IPA) and the
Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument (NDICI).
Grant agreements
In 2022 the EEA, together with the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA), the
European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) and the EC, developed a coordinated agency
contribution to the Horizon Europe Partnership for the Assessment of the Risks of
Chemicals (PARC). PARC is the successor to the human biomonitoring for Europe
(HBM4EU) Horizon 2020 project, which ended in June 2022 and in which the EEA
participated as a partner. The PARC grant agreement began in May 2022 and will run
for seven years.

3.1.1 EEA-Eionet Strategy to 2030 and its future directions
In December 2020, the EEA management board adopted a joint EEA-Eionet Strategy
for the period 2021-2030, ′Delivering data and knowledge to achieve Europe′s
environment and climate ambitions′. The strategy covers five areas of work:
• biodiversity and ecosystems;
• climate change mitigation and adaptation;
• human health and the environment;
• circular economy and resource use;
• sustainability trends, prospects and responses.
These are measured against five strategic objectives (SOs) to 2030 as described in
Table 3.1 below.
Given the large number of new activities and responsibilities assigned to the EEA
as part of the EGD initiatives, in spring 2024 the EEA management board initiated
a process of discussing the future directions of the EEA-Eionet Strategy to 2030.
The expectation is that the decision on adjustments to the EEA-Eionet Strategy
to 2030 will be finalised at the Management Board meeting on 4 December 2025.
Linked to that and the need to develop a simplified approach to how planning and
programming is presented to EEA stakeholders, in mid-2024 EEA senior management
initiated an internal process for updating the delivery model that sets out to articulate
how the EEA delivers the services it provides. A clear signal from the EC′s evaluation
of the EEA and Eionet (2017-2021) pointed towards the need to better document and
where necessary improve the ′efficiency′ of EEA operations, as well as the overview
and presentation of EEA activities.
The updated delivery model has been designed for greater transparency and to
enable management to set priorities in line with the demands of EEA stakeholders,
whilst also enabling an easy and direct understanding of resource allocation and
production. The increased focus on services channelled via the updated delivery
model requires that the EEA devotes attention to output types (products and
services), quality assurance, resource management and impact; these requirements
will be gradually introduced as the EEA rolls out the updated delivery model. This
model was implemented as part of the work programme structure in January 2025
and is reflected in the presentation of annual work programme activities in Section 4
of this single programming document (SPD). The structure is aligned to the EEA′s
core work areas in the following ways:

Details of the scope and coverage of activities for 2026 under the three core work

3.2.2 Eionet, EEA scientific committee and European Topic Centres (ETCs)
Eionet is a partnership network of the EEA and its member and cooperating countries,
connecting around 3,000 experts and 600 national environmental institutions. It
facilitates the collection and dissemination of environmental data and information
across Europe and provides environmental knowledge as a service for European and
national policymaking. Eionet supports the EEA in delivering timely, targeted, relevant
and reliable information to policymakers and the public. It consists of national focal
points (NFPs), Eionet groups, Eionet thematic and Eionet working groups and ETCs.

ETCs are a core part of the EEA-Eionet relationship. They act as a conduit for data
and information flows and analysis between the EU level and EEA member countries.

collection, verification and assessment of environmental and climate data that
Member States report under EU legislation and for which the EEA has responsibility.
ETCs contribute to the delivery of all four delivery model services (see Annex 13

100 organisations in EEA member countries with expertise in specific environmental
areas. Each ETC consists of a coordinating organisation and specialist partner
organisations. Many organisations are public sector bodies. The work of the ETC
consortia terminates at the end of 2026. During the course of 2026, new topic
centres will be designated by the management board.

3.2.4 Digital capabilities
The EEA digital capability strategy 2025-2030 was adopted by senior management in
spring 2025 after an extensive process involving EEA staff, management, Eionet and
other stakeholders. It was further discussed and commented on by the management
board during the 104th management board meeting in March 2025.
It is a comprehensive and forward-looking strategy for EEA-Eionet towards 2030
that guides the necessary investments in digital capabilities, transformation and
partnerships across technology, data, people and processes, with a multiannual
perspective. The strategy supports all the strategic objectives of the EEA-Eionet
strategy and aims to future-proof the work of the EEA and its network.
The senior management agreed upon the strategy′s adoption to allocate a multiannual
investment for implementation of the strategy during its implementation period
(2025-2030), with a budget amount to be agreed separately.
Investments in digital capabilities follow the six ′digital missions′ of the digital
capability strategy 2025-2030 and link directly to the new delivery model.

The EEA′s tasks have grown significantly under the current MFF, with a

Section 2.2 ′Development of new tasks′ lists and briefly describes the additional tasks

The staff posts specified in the legislative packages are almost entirely for

support posts. This has resulted in a substantial reduction in the ratio of support to
operational staff and placed an untenable burden on support functions. This problem
is elaborated in the Section 3.3.3 covering the agency request for 2026.
In accordance with the specification of the MFF 2021-2027, the EEA receives an
annual indexation of 2% to its EU subvention. Following the invasion of Ukraine,
inflation has significantly exceeded this; the four-year compound salary indexation
for EEA staff for 2022 to 2025 is 19%. To address the salary increases, the EC has
provided further reinforcement of the EEA′s EU subvention in 2023, 2024 and 2025,
to address the main budget pressures from salary increases. However, for both
this and the prior MFF, the expenditure on Title 1 (staff) and Title 2 (premises and
administration) is consuming an increasing portion of the EEA′s budget, reducing the
funds available for operations (Title 3).
3.3.2 Outlook for the years 2026-2028
In November the EC announced the annual salary indexation of +3.0%, and an
increase in the Denmark correlation coefficient from 129.8 to 130.5, to be applied
from 1 July 2025. The 2026 budget circular forecasts an indexation of +3.4% to be
applied from 1 July 2026. This translates into an effective annual indexation of 3.5%
from 2025 to 2026 and then 2.7% from 2026 to 2027.
In response, the EC has also topped up the standard 2% indexation of the EU

3.3.4 Strategy for achieving efficiency gains
The EEA continues to strive towards further efficiency gains through the
implementation of the five SOs of the current strategy which, in turn, influence
activities under three key work areas described in Section 3.1.
The benefits of the new delivery model include:
• efficiency improvements in budget allocations and spending;
• broader and more standardised use of digital tools for managing and
disseminating knowledge;
• increased impact and value creation by disseminating knowledge among users
more quickly;
• more support for stakeholders to enhance the inherent value proposition of the EEA
and Eionet (see Section 3.3.1 for further details).
In the pollution and health work area, the implementation of the revised Ambient
Air Quality Directive will require the development of a new data model for reporters
(based on a revised data reporting decision from the EC). This will also present an
opportunity to switch the data reporting to Reportnet 3. As part of this process,
opportunities will be explored to streamline reporting and increase the overall
efficiency of the data reporting, processing and publication process (for example,

The main drivers of the development in the EEA′s budgeted expenditure from 2024

Firstly, the additional resources allocated to the EEA via finance fiches, to deliver
new tasks defined by the Commission in several legislative packages. Overviews of
the legislative packages and associated resources are provided in Tables 11 and 12

Secondly, the impacts of inflationary increases: the Commission′s guidance for
budget development given for MFF 2021-27 had defined a 2% annual indexation
for the EEA′s EU subvention to give ′stability in real terms′ and the Commission
confirmed this instruction for the 2025 budget in the Budget Circular. However, this
has not been sufficient in the current inflationary environment, particularly regarding
increases in salaries. The Commission therefore has reinforced the budgets each
year since 2023 with additional funds, so exceeding the 2% annual indexation, to
provide additional funding for salaries, and included a further reinforcement of
EUR 555,000 in 2026. These reinforcements have significantly reduced the pressures
on the expenditure budget, but the proportion of the budget allocated to Title 1 and 2
has been steadily increasing, with a resultant reduction in the proportion of budget
available for operational expenditure (Title 3).
Some of the main expenditure developments are as follows:
• Chapter 11: The increase from 2025 to 2026 in the Budget Forecast is firstly,
firstly the result of the effective salary indexation from 2025 to 2026 of +3.5%.
Secondly, the 2026 budget includes salary expenditure for 21 new posts from new
five legislative packages (refer to Section 3.3 for details). The Agency Request
deviates from the Budget Forecast because it includes resources for five additional
temporary agent support posts which have been requested, calculated using the
standard rates specified by the Commission for new posts.
• The recruitment expenditure reflects the recruitment of new posts from legislative
packages and vacancies from normal staff turnover.
• The budget for Title 2 reflects the expenditure needed to run the EEA′s essential
office facilities, and staff IT and telephony services and equipment. The EEA is
currently converting its premises from individual office space to open activity-based
working space. This facilitates face-to-face collaboration, adjusts to the increased
teleworking and virtual collaboration, and provides greater flexibility. This has in turn
allowed for approximately 50% additional staff to be accommodated without an
increase in office space. This refurbishment was completed in 2025, with the last
large contracts having been placed in 2024, hence the reductions to the Chapter 21
and 22 budgets from 2024 to 2025.
• To leverage the benefits of shared services, the EEA increasingly makes use of
personnel, finance, procurement and IT security systems and services provided
by the Commission, which comprise most of the Chapter 23 budget. The budget
also covers the EEA′s governance structures, primarily its Management Board and
Scientific Committee (Chapter 25).

the grant agreements with seven European Topic Centres (ETCs), comprising
consortia of Member State institutions, which collaborate with the EEA in delivering
its work programme tasks. The budget also comprises expenditure for:
• its IT infrastructure and development to deliver its legislative dataflows,
systems and reporting obligations,
• its communication publications and outreach expenditure,
• expert meetings supporting in particular the European Environment Information
and Observation Network (Eionet), and

Annex 6 Environmental management
Context of the EEA and its environmental management strategy
Given the EEA′s mission and legal mandate, it recognises in its environment
policy that it has a special responsibility to act as a role model when it comes to
managing its own environmental performance. The EEA′s vision is to be a climate
neutral and resource-efficient organisation. To minimise its environmental impacts
and continually improve its performance, the EEA has in place an environmental
management system, which complies with the EMAS.
Overview of the EEA′s environmental management system
The EEA uses an environmental management system, which was registered
under EMAS in 2005. Since 2009, the EEA has published an annual environmental
statement on its website. EMAS is part of the EEA′s quality management
system. Environmental management, procedures, responsibilities and annual
activities are documented in the EEA environmental management handbook
(EEA internal document).
Environmental performances
The EEA achieved all its environmental targets for 2024, except in the area of
water consumption.
• The EEA′s environmental performance in 2024 showed no significant changes to
2023. The rebound effect compared to the years still influenced by the COVID-19
pandemic can no longer be seen. The statistics between 2022 and 2024 are
rather stable with some fluctuations related to the renovation of the premises on
Kongens Nytorv 6.
• The EEA′s electricity is 100% renewable and mainly powered by wind energy. 2024
showed a 7.8% reduction in energy consumption (electricity and heating). Over the
last 4 years, a decrease in staff related electricity consumption (total and per FTE)
was observed. The systematic use of energy efficient docking stations, as well
as the teleworking practices of staff and the deployment of the newly refurbished
areas of the building may have contributed to this. Changes in energy consumption
linked to heating could be associated with the renovation of two floors in Kongens
Nytorv 6 and a mild winter. Despite not being accounted for directly in the EEA′s
energy consumption, an increase was seen in the electricity consumption (+12%) of
the EEA′s IT server infrastructure, which has been co-located in an external, energy
efficient data centre since 2022.
• Paper consumption continued to decrease, with the ongoing digitalisation
of administrative workflows and the continued fall in printed materials. The
application of the zero-print policy for EEA publications continued, with no
discernible negative impact on outreach and the visibility of EEA products.

The EEA is organised as per the organisational chart (Annex 1) with six departments

The resources, both human and financial, are attributed to each department

The EEA governance bodies — the management board and bureau — adopt all

those related to the internal control system.
The EEA has decided to quality management to enhance internal efficiency and
quality towards end users and stakeholders. The quality management in the will
follow the ISO9001 methodology and approach. Implementation started towards
the end of 2024 and the implementation plan runs until the end of 2026. At this time,
main elements of the quality management should be in place. A project plan for
the implementation has been adopted following the initial phase of implementation
where training and key building blocks have been established supported by
Deloitte. When established, the quality management will be the overall framework
for monitoring and internal control via audits, a systematic approach to managing
deviations and KPIs.
For effective internal control, the EEA management board and bureau adopted
the EEA internal control framework at its 80th meeting in December 2017. This
framework derives from the internal control framework laid down by the EC for its
own departments.
In order to reinforce EEA internal control systems with the resources and
competences available, a decision has been made to change the internal audit
capability (IAC) function to an internal control coordinator (ICC) function, effective
from 1 January 2025. The main responsibilities of the ICC will cover many of
the advisory tasks currently performed by the IAC, with broader contributions,
monitoring and coordination. Active contributions, monitoring and coordination
for these advisory tasks were previously incompatible with the independence of
an internal auditor. This change does not affect the good governance of the EEA,
as it is audited every year by both the European Court of Auditors and the Internal
Audit Service, which is the ′internal auditor′ in the context of EEA financial regulation
(Chapter 7, Article 78 and Article 79).
The five components of the EEA internal control framework are as follows:
Control environment: Under this umbrella, EEA management has defined how the
organisation ensures a common approach regarding responsibility, accountability,
integrity and the competences of staff.
In particular, the EEA has put measures in place to prevent cases of conflict of
interest. The EEA′s degree of exposure to the risk of conflict of interest has been
assessed in the policy for the management and prevention of conflicts of interest
and reputational risk. Some of the existing mitigating measures to respond to the
risks listed in the policy are as follow:

subject to any conditions it thinks fit.
Risk management: EEA management identifies risks to the achievement of its
objectives across the organisation after setting the EEA mission, objectives per
activity, financial objectives, reporting and monitoring. Risk identification and
assessment are done every quarter at the project level and annually at the EEA level.
The risk of fraud is considered for each of these assessments. However, it is formally
assessed every three years when the anti-fraud strategy is reviewed or when relevant
changes occur in the EEA organisation within the three years. The EEA management
board adopted the first anti-fraud strategy and action plan in November 2014 and has
adopted the regular updates thereafter. A revision is planned for 2025, when a new
action plan will be defined.
Control activities: Several control procedures have been developed to mitigate the
risks identified in the risk management exercises and to mitigate the risks inherent
to EEA activities. Among these procedures, the EEA management has defined user
rights so that segregation of duties is respected both in the approval processes and
in IT systems. IT governance structures and workflows are well established.
Information and communication: This component of the EEA internal control system
relates to both internal and external measures put in place. Regular staff meetings
are conducted by the EEA executive director and decision lists taken from the senior
management team meetings are available to all staff. In the case of concerns about
fraud or serious wrongdoing, EEA staff can access procedures to help them raise
their concerns in an adequate way to the appropriate functions. These functions keep
their information on procedures updated, with their participation in targeted networks
on internal control.
For external communication, specific communication strategies are developed to
ensure that the messages are relevant to the audience being targeted and are cost-
effective. Regular contact takes place between the EEA and the EC to align their
messages about the environment or common projects.

The EEA′s international engagement is firmly anchored in the founding regulation

partners on data and the development of indicators, methodologies as well as
